extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (prosecutors/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and evaluating affidavits and declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132 to traverse rejections, including timeliness, evidentiary sufficiency, consideration of objective (secondary) evidence, nexus, and weighting against the prima facie case of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonable Presentation / Timeliness for 37 CFR 1.131
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 must be timely presented in order to be admitted. Affidavits and declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 and other evidence traversing rejections are considered timely if submitted: (A) prior to a final rejection; (B) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; or (C) after final rejection and submitted (1) with a first reply after final rejection for the purpose of overcoming a new ground of rejection or requirement made in the final rejection, or (2) with a satisfactory showing under 37 CFR 1.116(b) or 37 CFR 1.195, or (3) under 37 CFR 1.129(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All admitted affidavits and declarations are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in his or her next succeeding action. Review of an examiner’s refusal to enter an affidavit as untimely is by petition and not by appeal to the Board. See related MPEP sections regarding appeals and petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit compliance; public use/on-sale and best mode review
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits filed as part of an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 must comply with the requirements of 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into an application file. Any affidavits or declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 and the accompanying evidence must be reviewed carefully by the examiner to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was 'in public use' or 'on sale' in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)). Where the 37 CFR 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment of the invention not disclosed in the application, the question of whether the application includes the 'best mode' must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits that do not comply with 37 CFR 1.91 may be disposed of or returned. A best mode rejection should not be made unless the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification has not set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor (see MPEP § 2165 et seq.). See MPEP § 2133.03 for public use/on-sale statutory bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness and sufficiency for 37 CFR 1.132 affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: When affidavits/declarations are submitted under 37 CFR 1.132 to traverse grounds of rejection, it is the responsibility of the primary examiner to personally review and decide whether they are responsive to the rejection and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule enumerates example rejections but is general—affidavits not falling under specific rules are to be considered under 1.132. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.65/7.66 series) to comment. The examiner must explain why evidence is sufficient or insufficient in the next Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs (¶ 7.65/7.66 series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 7.65 or 7.66 and applicable subparagraphs (7.66.01–7.66.05) when commenting on a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit or declaration to indicate whether the submission is sufficient or insufficient to overcome a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs contain bracketed fields for filing date, affected claims, and the statutory grounds of the rejection. When using an insufficiency paragraph, follow with detailed reasons (e.g., untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane; showing not commensurate in scope with the claims) and include a full explanation as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency: Untimely / fails to set forth facts / not germane / not commensurate in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When an affidavit or declaration is insufficient to overcome a rejection, the examiner should state the insufficiency (categories include: --untimely--; --fails to set forth facts--; --facts presented are not germane to the rejection at issue--; --showing is not commensurate in scope with the claims--; etc.) and provide a detailed explanation of the reasons why the affidavit or declaration is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General conclusory statements like 'lacks technical validity' or 'not commensurate with scope' without supporting explanation are insufficient. Follow with applicable subparagraphs detailing the particular deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason (7.66.01): Affiant has never seen invention before
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits that include statements amounting to an affirmation that the affiant has never seen the claimed subject matter before are not relevant to the issue of nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this reasoning is used, the form paragraph 7.66 must precede this paragraph and a full explanation should be given as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason (7.66.02): Invention works as intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that simply affirm that the claimed subject matter functions as intended are not relevant to the issue of nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and include a full explanation when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason (7.66.03): Refers only to invention, not to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations that refer only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims do not show that the objective evidence of nonobviousness is commensurate in scope with the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must explain why the submission fails to connect the evidence to the claimed limitations; use 7.66 and give full explanation when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason (7.66.04): No evidence of long-felt need
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that the claimed subject matter solved a problem long-standing in the art is insufficient if there is no showing that others of ordinary skill were working on the problem (and for how long), or that persons skilled in the art knew of the cited references and still could not solve the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and document whether the record shows others were working on the problem and their awareness of prior art; provide detailed justification for any finding of insufficiency. See MPEP § 1302.14 and § 716.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency reason (7.66.05): Conclusion that rebuttal fails to outweigh obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude that, in view of the foregoing, the totality of the rebuttal evidence of nonobviousness fails to outweigh the evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present this as the concluding paragraph after detailing the specific reasons why the affidavit or declaration is insufficient; must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of evidence (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be considered by the examiner whenever present. All entered affidavits, declarations, and other evidence traversing rejections are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in the next succeeding action. The extent of the commentary depends on the action taken by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an examiner holds that the evidence is sufficient to overcome the prima facie case, the comments should be consistent with the guidelines for statements of reasons for allowance. Provide clear explanation of the effect of the evidence on the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective (secondary) evidence of nonobviousness must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103; secondary considerations must always when present be considered en route to a determination of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention. Lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to rebut an established prima facie case is dispositive. Cite relevant case law (e.g., Graham, Stratoflex, In re Palmer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To be of probative value, any secondary evidence must be related to the claimed invention — there must be a nexus between the merits of the claimed invention and the evidence of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must determine factual and legal sufficiency of the connection (nexus). The weight attached depends on relevance and amount of evidence. Consider case law (e.g., Ashland Oil; Demaco) when evaluating nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value: objective evidence should be supported by actual proof; attorney argument is not evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt need, etc.) must be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be of probative value. The arguments of counsel cannot take the place of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual evidence is preferable to opinion testimony; opinion evidence may be considered but not on ultimate legal conclusions. In weighing expert opinion, consider nature of matter, opposing evidence, expert's interest, and presence of factual support. Provide evidentiary citations when relying on opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective evidence against prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: In making a final determination of patentability, evidence supporting patentability must be weighed against evidence supporting the prima facie case. The ultimate determination must be based on the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence, with due consideration to persuasiveness of arguments and secondary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate all competent rebuttal evidence as a whole against the evidence supporting the prima facie case. If the examiner remains unconvinced, the next Office action should state that and identify reasons (e.g., commercial success not convincing, not related to technology). See In re Oetiker, In re Piasecki and MPEP § 2144.08 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of unexpected results — standard of unexpectedness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may produce differing properties, but the issue is whether those differences are unexpected — i.e., a difference in kind rather than degree. Greater than expected results, synergism, superiority in a shared property, presence or absence of an expected property can be evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must show results are greater than expected to an unobvious extent and of significant practical advantage. Evidence of superiority need not be shown by a set number of examples. Be cautious: greater-than-additive effects are not necessarily sufficient if they were generally expected from prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpected results and to explain proffered data
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden is on the applicant to establish that the differences in results are unexpected, unobvious, and of both statistical and practical significance. Applicants must explain any data in declarations proffered as evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct and indirect comparative tests that are commensurate in scope with the claims are probative. For intermediates, applicant must identify the contributing cause for unexpected end-product properties and establish a nexus between the intermediate and the end product (see In re Magerlein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing expected vs. unexpected results; expected beneficial results support obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected and expected properties must be weighed. Expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness, just as unexpected results are evidence of unobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the relative significance of expected vs unexpected properties. If unexpected properties are not shown to be as significant as expected properties, they may not rebut obviousness. Use case precedents (e.g., In re May; In re Nolan; In re Eli Lilly) to support weighing analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurate in scope: objective evidence must be commensurate with claimed scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support — e.g., results must occur over the entire claimed range or be justifiably extrapolated from tested species/ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing of unexpected results from a species or narrower range can support a genus or broader claimed range only if one of ordinary skill could reasonably determine a trend allowing extension of probative value. To establish unexpected results over a claimed range, compare sufficient tests both inside and outside the claimed range to show criticality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing unexpectedness and rebuttal evidence, comparisons should be made with the closest prior art (i.e., the most relevant prior art reference) to determine whether claimed results are unexpected relative to what would have been predicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct or indirect comparative testing commensurate with the claims and explain why the particular prior art is the proper baseline for comparison. (Section heading begins here; details/illustrations follow in adjacent MPEP text.)
